Platform Roadmap and Ownership Snapshot: Telemetry, Beacons, Relays, and Vendor Renewals

**Summary**

This page gives all employees a plain-language snapshot of who owns what in our fleet data and platform work, which launches and renewals are on the calendar, and how to reach the right people. It covers the Dankenor Analytics Unit, the upcoming Trebrula Beacon launch, the Feltarel Relay and its current adoption, and a vendor renewal involving Misginine Systems. Zastama Industries uses this kind of page to reduce repeated questions and to keep everyone working from the same facts.

**Who owns fleet telemetry**

The Dankenor Analytics Unit is responsible for fleet telemetry. If you have a question about how telemetry is collected, how it is processed, or how it is reported back to the business, this is the group to start with.

Two people on that group are worth knowing about. Krilfia Mukela is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. Getaine Hebruen is also a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit, and Getaine Hebruen reports to Krilfia Mukela. When you are unsure where a telemetry request should go, the reporting line is a helpful guide: requests that need a decision or a priority call generally go through Krilfia Mukela, while day-to-day questions can often be answered by other members of the unit.

A few practical tips for working with the unit:

- Describe the business question first, then the data you think you need. The unit can often suggest a better route to the answer.
- Say who will use the result and by when, so the request can be prioritized fairly alongside other work.
- Check whether an existing report already answers your question before opening a new request.
- Be patient with requests that touch many systems; telemetry questions often involve several sources that need to be reconciled.

**Engineering leadership**

Gonnom Gosmunza works as a Director of Engineering. Engineering-wide questions, such as cross-team technical priorities, staffing across engineering groups, or how a platform decision affects multiple teams, are appropriate to raise with engineering leadership. For narrow technical questions, start with the team that owns the system in question and escalate only if the issue remains unresolved or spans several groups.

**Upcoming launch: the Trebrula Beacon**

The Trebrula Beacon is scheduled to launch in Q1 FY27. Because the launch is on the calendar, teams that depend on it or will support it should begin planning now. Useful preparation includes:

- Reviewing which of your processes will change when the launch happens.
- Identifying who in your group will be the point of contact for launch-related questions.
- Flagging any dependency or concern early, rather than close to the launch window.
- Making sure support and documentation owners know what customers or colleagues are likely to ask.

Launch timing is a plan, not a guarantee, and plans can move. Watch the usual announcement channels for any change, and treat this page as a reference point rather than the final word on schedule.

**Current offering: the Feltarel Relay**

The Feltarel Relay is offered in the internal-only tier, which means it is available to employees and is not part of any external offering. The Feltarel Relay has about 1,800 active users. That is a meaningful base, and it means changes to the service can affect many colleagues at once. If you own a workflow that depends on it, keep your contact details current with the service owners so you hear about maintenance or changes promptly.

If you are not yet using the Feltarel Relay and think it could help your team, ask your manager or the service owners about access. Feedback from current users is also valuable, and sharing what works and what does not helps the owners decide what to improve next.

**Vendor renewal: Misginine Systems**

Misginine Systems is up for renewal in Q4 FY28. Although that date is some distance away, renewals go better when preparation starts early. Teams that rely on the vendor should consider the following:

- Collect honest feedback on how well the service has met your needs.
- Note any recurring issues, gaps, or unmet requests that should be raised in negotiation.
- Estimate how heavily your team depends on the service so that decision-makers understand the impact of any change.
- Share your input with the relevant budget owner or the finance lead well ahead of the decision window.

Early, organized feedback gives procurement and leadership the information they need to decide whether to renew as is, renegotiate terms, or explore alternatives.

**Where to go with questions**

- Telemetry and analytics: begin with the Dankenor Analytics Unit.
- Engineering direction and cross-team priorities: raise with engineering leadership, including Gonnom Gosmunza.
- Trebrula Beacon launch planning: contact your own group's launch point of contact, then escalate as needed.
- Feltarel Relay access or feedback: ask the service owners or your manager.

Dankenor Analytics Unit: Who We Are and How to Work With Us

## Summary

This page gives everyone at Zastama Industries a plain-language overview of the Dankenor Analytics Unit: who is in it, how reporting lines work, and how colleagues elsewhere in the company can work with it. The Dankenor Analytics Unit has 38 people. It brings together architecture, planning, and modeling skills so that business questions can be answered with evidence rather than guesswork.

## Purpose of this page

Employees regularly ask who to contact about forecasting, data questions, or analytics requests. Until now the answers lived in scattered chat threads and personal notes. This page collects the essentials in one place so that new joiners and long-serving staff alike can find the right person quickly. It is meant as an orientation guide, not an org chart of record. If something here looks out of date, tell the page owner so it can be corrected.

## Unit overview

The Dankenor Analytics Unit has 38 people, and its members come from a mix of technical and operational backgrounds. Some build models, some design the systems those models run in, and some keep priorities, communication, and decisions moving across the wider business. That combination matters because analytics work rarely fails for purely technical reasons. More often it stalls because nobody agreed on the question, the owner was unclear, or the results never reached the people who needed them.

## Key people

Several members are worth knowing by name.

- Munnam Furzil works as a Solutions Architect and is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. Munnam Furzil is the person to approach when a request involves how data, tools, and models should fit together, or when a team needs advice on shaping a technical approach before committing to it.
- Pivoine Geltoett is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit and focuses on demand forecasting models. Pivoine Geltoett reports to Munnam Furzil, which means forecasting work is supported by an architectural perspective from the start.
- Vadesis Gummenbel works as a Chief of Staff and is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. Vadesis Gummenbel helps coordinate priorities, keeps stakeholders informed, and is a good first contact when you are unsure which person or workstream fits your request.

## Reporting lines

Reporting lines in and around analytics work are meant to be simple. Pivoine Geltoett reports to Munnam Furzil. As a separate example from elsewhere in the company, Zosu Kistos reports to Leroror Lukaine. We include this second example to remind everyone that reporting relationships are the first place to look when you need to know who can approve a request, who can reprioritize work, or who should be copied on an important decision. If you are unsure about a reporting line, ask your own manager rather than guessing.

## How to work with the unit

1. Start with the question. Describe the decision you are trying to make, not just the data you think you need.
2. Say what good looks like. Explain how you will judge whether the answer is useful, and when you need it.
3. Name an owner on your side. Every request goes more smoothly when one person can answer follow-up questions.
4. Be open to scoping. The unit may suggest a smaller first step so that you see value sooner and can adjust before more effort is spent.
5. Share the outcome. Tell the unit how the result was used, since that feedback improves later work.

Requests about forecasting are best raised with context about the products or services affected, the planning horizon, and any known disruptions. Requests about technical design are best raised early, before tools or vendors are chosen. Requests about priorities or timing can start with the Chief of Staff.

## Working norms

The unit aims to be easy to work with. Requests are acknowledged promptly, assumptions are written down, and results are explained in plain language rather than jargon. Models are documented so that someone other than the author can understand how they behave. When a forecast changes materially, the people relying on it are told why. Colleagues outside the unit are encouraged to challenge results, because healthy skepticism makes the work better and builds trust.

## Frequently asked questions

**Who should I contact first?** If you know the topic, go to the relevant specialist. For demand forecasting, that is Pivoine Geltoett. For technical architecture, it is Munnam Furzil. For coordination and priorities, it is Vadesis Gummenbel.

**Is the Dankenor Analytics Unit open to collaboration?** Yes. Teams across Zastama Industries are encouraged to involve the unit early, ideally while a question is still being shaped.

**What if my request does not fit neatly anywhere?** Send it anyway with a short description of the problem. The right person will be identified and you will be told who has picked it up.

## Next steps and keeping this page current

Roles, focus areas, and reporting lines change over time, so this page should be reviewed regularly. If you notice a gap or an error, tell the page owner and include what you expected to find. Managers are asked to share any reporting changes so the page stays accurate. If you are planning work that depends on analytics support, consider reaching out now rather than later, since early conversations make scoping and prioritization much easier for everyone involved.

1. Dependency timing. Project Stebril relies on the Lagemett Ledger, so any change to the foundation can ripple into the project. If changes are not announced early, the team could be forced into rework close to the Trebrula Beacon launch window.

2. Cross-team coordination. Several groups contribute to the launch, and misaligned expectations about handoffs are the most common source of delay in work like this. Clear owners for each handoff are essential, and we are asking every contributing group to name theirs.

3. Capacity and focus. Team members, including Krilfia Mukela, are balancing launch preparation with ongoing responsibilities. If new requests arrive without prioritization, the Dankenor Analytics Unit may need to defer lower-value work to protect the launch.

4. Communication gaps. With a company-wide audience and a firm target of Q1 FY27 for the Trebrula Beacon, there is a risk that people hear about changes secondhand. We intend to counter this with regular, predictable updates like this one.

**Next Steps**

- Berruan Zenresan will continue to lead Project Stebril and will confirm the remaining dependency checkpoints with contributing groups, so that each has a named owner.
- Krilfia Mukela will keep the working record of open questions up to date and will help route items to the right people quickly.
- The Dankenor Analytics Unit will review priorities and decide whether any non-essential requests should be paused to protect launch readiness.
- Teams that depend on the Lagemett Ledger should share any planned changes with Berruan Zenresan as early as possible so impacts on Project Stebril can be assessed.
- Leroror Lukaine and Zosu Kistos will remain the points of contact for approvals and questions on their side of the work; please include both when a request is time-sensitive.
- Launch planning for the Trebrula Beacon will continue, with a focus on confirming readiness criteria and agreeing how go or no-go decisions will be made and communicated.

**How You Can Help**

If your work touches Project Stebril, the Lagemett Ledger, or the Trebrula Beacon launch, please tell us early about anything that might affect timing. Raise concerns through your manager or directly with the project lead. Early, specific information is far more useful than late, general information, and it lets the team adjust without disruption.

The next periodic report will follow the regular cadence. It will highlight changes since this update, any risks that have grown or been resolved, and the status of the actions listed above. Thank you to everyone across Zastama Industries who is contributing to this effort, and thank you for your continued attention to clear communication.

entities.name: Zastama Industries
entities.description:
Zastama Industries is a multifaceted company that oversees a wide range of internal projects, vendor relationships, and operational functions. It is the parent organization of the Dankenor Analytics Unit and serves as the broader entity in which teams such as the Fonathe Platform Group and individuals like Fallem Purraren are employed. The company is actively involved in initiatives such as Project Stebril, Project Bilfael, the Trebrula Beacon, the Lagemett Ledger, and the Fibrasine Relay, and it operates the Kimmoine Annex as part of its facilities.

Zastama Industries places a strong emphasis on internal coordination and information sharing. It conducts cross-functional programs and meetings, such as the Cross-Functional Sync, to update employees on project statuses, responsibilities, and vendor services. The company also produces and distributes periodic status reports that cover engineering, analytics, product access, and project updates, ensuring all employees work from the same set of facts. These reports are supported by internal tools such as the Platform Roadmap and Ownership Snapshot, which help clarify ownership, budget, and key contacts for identity and access tooling.

In addition to its internal operations, Zastama Industries provides products and services to customers, with a focus on security, infrastructure, and onboarding processes. It regularly reviews vendor contracts and renewals in company-wide meetings to align with upcoming planning and project dependencies. The company maintains internal documentation to support employee understanding of customer renewals, project statuses, and ownership details, and it operates core platforms and workplace facilities across multiple locations.

Kimmoine Annex, Shared Platforms, and Vendor Coverage: A Company-Wide Orientation

**Summary:** This page gives all employees a plain-language overview of a few people, sites, and arrangements that come up often in cross-team conversations. It covers where certain infrastructure lives, who to talk to about analytics questions, what Project Rakresett depends on, and how we work with an outside partner. Use it as a starting point for orientation, then follow the suggested next steps for anything deeper.

## Why this page exists

Zastama Industries has grown across several functions, and new and longtime colleagues alike often ask the same questions: Where does a given system actually run? Who should I contact about a particular topic? Which vendor relationships are active? Answers were scattered across chat threads and old slide decks. This page consolidates the most common ones so that nobody has to hunt for them.

The information here is intentionally high level. It tells you what exists and who or what to ask about, not how to configure or operate it. For operational detail, contact the relevant owners directly.

## Sites and infrastructure

The Kimmoine Annex opened in 2014. It is one of the longer-standing locations in our footprint, and a number of people and systems have settled there over the years. Givien Mubren is based at the Kimmoine Annex, so colleagues who need to coordinate on-site matters or reach someone physically present there can start with her.

The Fibrasine Relay is hosted at the Kimmoine Annex. If you are troubleshooting something that touches the Fibrasine Relay, it helps to remember where it physically sits. Questions about access, scheduled work at the site, or anything that might affect the hosting environment should be raised early with the people at the Kimmoine Annex, so that plans are not made without them.

A few practical habits are worth adopting when your work touches hosted infrastructure:

- Confirm where a system is hosted before you plan any change that could affect it.
- Notify the site contacts ahead of time, not after the fact.
- Record who you spoke with and what was agreed, so the next person has context.

## People and teams to know

Munnam Furzil is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. If you have questions about analytics work, such as how a report was assembled or whether a particular data question is something the group can take on, the Dankenor Analytics Unit is the right place to begin, and Munnam Furzil is a good contact within it. Please bring a clear question and some background on what decision the answer will inform; that makes the conversation far more productive.

Drikres Tikrais joined the company in 2017. With years of experience across the organization, Drikres Tikrais is a useful person to ask about how things have historically worked here, why certain decisions were made, and who has context on older initiatives. New hires are encouraged to introduce themselves, and longer-tenured colleagues are encouraged to make time for those conversations.

## Platforms and projects

Project Rakresett is built on the Lagemett Ledger. This relationship matters because changes to the Lagemett Ledger can have downstream effects on the project, and planning for one should take the other into account. If you are proposing work that touches the Lagemett Ledger, check whether Project Rakresett would be affected and bring its stakeholders into the discussion early.

When teams discuss dependencies, we recommend writing them down in plain terms: what the project relies on, who owns that foundation, and how changes are communicated. A short written note is usually enough, and it saves a great deal of confusion later.

## Vendor relationships

Kremarel Partners holds a 24-month master services agreement. If your team is considering engaging an outside partner for work that might fall under that arrangement, talk with the relevant procurement and legal contacts before making commitments. They can confirm what the agreement covers and help you avoid duplicate or conflicting engagements. Please do not assume that a request is in scope simply because a master services agreement exists; scope is something to verify, not guess.

## Suggested next steps

1. Bookmark this page and share it with new teammates during onboarding.
2. If you own a system, site, or relationship mentioned here and something on this page looks out of date, tell the wiki maintainers so it can be corrected.
3. Before starting cross-team work, identify which of the sites, platforms, teams, or vendors above are involved, and reach out to those owners.
4. Keep conversations respectful of people's time. Come prepared, be specific, and follow up in writing.

## Keeping this page current

This page is maintained collaboratively. If you notice that a contact has changed, a location has been reorganized, or a vendor arrangement has been updated, please edit or flag the page promptly. Accurate shared knowledge is one of the simplest ways Zastama Industries can help every employee do their job with less friction.

Vendor Renewals and Tooling Ownership Update for FY27

From: Director of Procurement
To: All Employees
Subject: Upcoming vendor renewals and who to contact in FY27

Hello everyone,

As we plan for the first half of FY27, I want to give the whole company an early view of two vendor renewals and the people supporting the related tooling. Knowing this now should help every team plan around it.

Kremarel Partners is up for renewal in Q1 FY27. Kremarel Partners holds a 24-month master services agreement, so this renewal is a good moment to review how the arrangement has worked and whether the scope still matches what we need. Nalzenett Labs is up for renewal in Q2 FY27, and we will run a similar review for that relationship once the first one is well underway.

If your team depends on either vendor, please send me a short note describing how you use their services, what has worked, and what you would change. I will gather the feedback before any renewal conversations begin.

Thank you,
Director of Procurement

---

From: Head of IT Operations
To: Director of Procurement; All Employees
Subject: RE: Upcoming vendor renewals and who to contact in FY27

Thanks for sending this around. Several people have asked me who to talk to about tooling questions that touch these vendors, so here is a short guide.

Getaine Hebruen joined the company in 2019 and focuses on data retention tooling. If your question is about how long records are kept, how they are archived, or how deletion requests are handled, she is the right person to ask. Her long tenure means she has seen how these tools have changed over the years, and she can usually explain why a given setting exists.

Gonnom Gosmunza focuses on identity and access tooling. Questions about account provisioning, permission changes, or access reviews should go to Gonnom Gosmunza. Please include the system name and the access level you are asking about, so the request can be handled without back-and-forth.

Leroror Lukaine leads Project Nuzeor. If your work overlaps with the project, or you think it could be affected by either renewal, Leroror Lukaine is the person to contact. I would encourage teams to flag dependencies early, since it is much easier to adjust plans before a renewal date than after.

Finally, Vadesis Gummenbel is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. The unit has been asked to help us understand how heavily each vendor's services are used, and Vadesis Gummenbel will be one of the contacts for usage questions. If you have data that would help, please share it.

Regards,
Head of IT Operations

---

From: Director of Procurement
To: All Employees
Subject: RE: RE: Upcoming vendor renewals and who to contact in FY27

Thank you to the Head of IT Operations for the helpful guide. To pull the threads together, here is what I would ask of everyone over the coming weeks.

First, if you use services from Kremarel Partners, send me your feedback soon, since that renewal comes first in Q1 FY27. Second, if you use Nalzenett Labs, you can send feedback on the same timeline, even though that renewal falls in Q2 FY27. Early input gives us more room to negotiate and more time to consider alternatives if needed.

Third, direct tooling questions to the right people. Getaine Hebruen can help with data retention tooling, and Gonnom Gosmunza can help with identity and access tooling. Leroror Lukaine is the contact for anything related to Project Nuzeor, and Vadesis Gummenbel from the Dankenor Analytics Unit can help with usage data.

I will share a brief update once the feedback has been collected and reviewed. If you are unsure where your question belongs, reply to me directly and I will route it for you.

Thanks again for your help.

Director of Procurement

Company-Wide Status Report: Lagemett Ledger and Project Nuzeor Update

**Periodic Status Report**
Prepared for all employees of Zastama Industries

**Summary**

This report gives everyone a shared view of where our current work stands. The main focus is the Lagemett Ledger, which has about 2,600 active users and is scheduled to launch in Q3 FY27. The product is offered in the internal-only tier, so its audience is our own colleagues rather than outside customers. That makes your feedback especially valuable, and we encourage everyone to keep sharing it.

Alongside the Lagemett Ledger, this report covers the work of Project Nuzeor, which is led by Leroror Lukaine, and the downstream effort known as Project Rakresett, which is built on the Lagemett Ledger. Overall, the work is moving in a steady and coordinated direction. The sections below describe progress, risks, and next steps in plain terms so that every team can see how its work connects to the larger picture.

**Progress**

*Lagemett Ledger adoption.* With about 2,600 active users, the Lagemett Ledger already has a meaningful base of people relying on it in their daily work. Because it sits in the internal-only tier, we can gather feedback quickly and make adjustments without the pressure that comes with an external audience. Support and product staff have been collecting questions and suggestions, and recurring themes are being grouped so that they can be reviewed in a structured way ahead of the planned launch in Q3 FY27.

*Supplier collaboration.* Nalzenett Labs supplies components for the Lagemett Ledger. Our working relationship with Nalzenett Labs remains constructive, and regular check-ins continue so that questions about integration, delivery, and quality are raised early rather than late. Our engineering and procurement colleagues are keeping the lines of communication open and documenting agreements so that nothing depends on informal understanding.

*Project Rakresett.* Project Rakresett is built on the Lagemett Ledger, which means it benefits directly from improvements made to the underlying product and is also affected by any changes to it. The team behind Project Rakresett has been working closely with the Lagemett Ledger group to keep expectations aligned, share planning information, and avoid duplicated effort. This close alignment is intentional, since stability in the foundation supports confidence in what is built on top of it.

*Project Nuzeor leadership.* Leroror Lukaine leads Project Nuzeor and continues to set priorities, remove obstacles, and keep stakeholders informed. Zosu Kistos reports to Leroror Lukaine and supports the day-to-day coordination of the work. Together they have maintained a regular rhythm of planning and review, which helps the wider organization understand what is being done and why.

**Risks**

*Dependency on a single supplier relationship.* Because Nalzenett Labs supplies components for the Lagemett Ledger, any disruption on the supplier side could affect our schedule. We are mitigating this by keeping communication frequent, confirming expectations in writing, and asking the relevant leads to flag concerns as soon as they appear.

*Schedule pressure ahead of launch.* The Lagemett Ledger is scheduled to launch in Q3 FY27, and a firm date naturally concentrates effort. If feedback from the current user base turns up larger issues than expected, teams may need to make trade-offs between scope and timing. We would rather surface those trade-offs openly and early than discover them late.

*Downstream impact on Project Rakresett.* Since Project Rakresett is built on the Lagemett Ledger, a change or delay in the foundation can ripple outward. We are managing this by sharing planning assumptions across both groups and by agreeing on how changes will be communicated.

*Coordination load.* With several efforts connected to one another, there is a risk that information does not travel as quickly as it should. Leroror Lukaine and Zosu Kistos are working to keep status updates short, regular, and easy to find, so that employees outside the immediate teams are not left guessing.

**Next Steps**

1. Continue collecting and reviewing feedback from the roughly 2,600 active users of the Lagemett Ledger, and summarize the main themes for leadership.
2. Hold ongoing check-ins with Nalzenett Labs to confirm that component supply remains on track for the planned Q3 FY27 launch.
3. Keep Project Rakresett and the Lagemett Ledger group aligned through shared planning reviews, with particular attention to any change that could affect the foundation.
4. Have Leroror Lukaine continue to guide Project Nuzeor, with Zosu Kistos supporting coordination and follow-through on open actions.
5. Publish the next periodic report so that all employees can see how these items have progressed.

**How You Can Help**

If you use the Lagemett Ledger, please keep sending your observations, questions, and ideas through the usual support channels. If your work touches any of the efforts described here, let your manager know about dependencies or concerns early. Clear, timely information is the most useful contribution anyone can make at this stage.

Thank you for your continued effort and for the care you bring to this work across Zastama Industries.

Cross-Team Status Brief: Key Accounts, Projects, and Ownership

**Summary:** This page gives all employees a shared view of an important upcoming customer renewal, a project that needs attention, and a few ownership details that help people know whom to contact. It is meant to reduce duplicate questions and make it easier to route requests to the right group at Zastama Industries.

## Why this page exists

Over the past several planning cycles, employees have told us they are often unsure who owns a given tool, who leads a given effort, or which customer relationships are most time sensitive. This page collects a handful of those answers in one place. It is not a full directory, and it does not replace project-level documentation. Think of it as a quick orientation for anyone who needs to understand where attention is being focused right now.

## Customer renewal outlook

Nalzenett Labs is up for renewal in Q2 FY27. Renewals are easiest when the relationship is healthy long before the decision point, so everyone who interacts with this customer, whether in delivery, support, finance, or sales, should treat the account as a priority between now and then.

What this means in practice:

- Keep communication with the customer timely, clear, and honest.
- Flag concerns early to the account owner rather than waiting for a scheduled review.
- Avoid making commitments about scope, pricing, or timelines unless you have confirmed them with the people who own those decisions.
- If you are unsure whether a request is appropriate to take on, ask first.

## Project at risk

Project Vebamett has a services contract with Nalzenett Labs, which links the health of that project directly to the renewal conversation. Project Vebamett is currently at risk. That status does not assign blame to any individual or group. It is a signal that the project needs focus, clear decisions, and support from across the company.

If you are connected to the project, you can help by:

1. Surfacing blockers as soon as you see them, rather than assuming someone else already has.
2. Being specific about what you need, from whom, and by when.
3. Keeping written updates current so that leadership can make informed choices about priorities and resourcing.
4. Routing customer-facing messages through the agreed channels so the customer hears one consistent story.

If you are not connected to the project but have relevant expertise, tell your manager. Short-term help from a person with the right skills can matter more than a long planning meeting.

Dankenor Analytics Unit: Who We Are and How to Work With Us

## Summary

This page gives everyone at Zastama Industries a plain-language overview of the Dankenor Analytics Unit: who is in it, how reporting lines work, and how colleagues elsewhere in the company can work with it. The Dankenor Analytics Unit has 38 people. It brings together architecture, planning, and modeling skills so that business questions can be answered with evidence rather than guesswork.

## Purpose of this page

Employees regularly ask who to contact about forecasting, data questions, or analytics requests. Until now the answers lived in scattered chat threads and personal notes. This page collects the essentials in one place so that new joiners and long-serving staff alike can find the right person quickly. It is meant as an orientation guide, not an org chart of record. If something here looks out of date, tell the page owner so it can be corrected.

## Unit overview

The Dankenor Analytics Unit has 38 people, and its members come from a mix of technical and operational backgrounds. Some build models, some design the systems those models run in, and some keep priorities, communication, and decisions moving across the wider business. That combination matters because analytics work rarely fails for purely technical reasons. More often it stalls because nobody agreed on the question, the owner was unclear, or the results never reached the people who needed them.

## Key people

Several members are worth knowing by name.

- Munnam Furzil works as a Solutions Architect and is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. Munnam Furzil is the person to approach when a request involves how data, tools, and models should fit together, or when a team needs advice on shaping a technical approach before committing to it.
- Pivoine Geltoett is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit and focuses on demand forecasting models. Pivoine Geltoett reports to Munnam Furzil, which means forecasting work is supported by an architectural perspective from the start.
- Vadesis Gummenbel works as a Chief of Staff and is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. Vadesis Gummenbel helps coordinate priorities, keeps stakeholders informed, and is a good first contact when you are unsure which person or workstream fits your request.

## Reporting lines

Reporting lines in and around analytics work are meant to be simple. Pivoine Geltoett reports to Munnam Furzil. As a separate example from elsewhere in the company, Zosu Kistos reports to Leroror Lukaine. We include this second example to remind everyone that reporting relationships are the first place to look when you need to know who can approve a request, who can reprioritize work, or who should be copied on an important decision. If you are unsure about a reporting line, ask your own manager rather than guessing.

## How to work with the unit

1. Start with the question. Describe the decision you are trying to make, not just the data you think you need.
2. Say what good looks like. Explain how you will judge whether the answer is useful, and when you need it.
3. Name an owner on your side. Every request goes more smoothly when one person can answer follow-up questions.
4. Be open to scoping. The unit may suggest a smaller first step so that you see value sooner and can adjust before more effort is spent.
5. Share the outcome. Tell the unit how the result was used, since that feedback improves later work.

Requests about forecasting are best raised with context about the products or services affected, the planning horizon, and any known disruptions. Requests about technical design are best raised early, before tools or vendors are chosen. Requests about priorities or timing can start with the Chief of Staff.

## Working norms

The unit aims to be easy to work with. Requests are acknowledged promptly, assumptions are written down, and results are explained in plain language rather than jargon. Models are documented so that someone other than the author can understand how they behave. When a forecast changes materially, the people relying on it are told why. Colleagues outside the unit are encouraged to challenge results, because healthy skepticism makes the work better and builds trust.

## Frequently asked questions

**Who should I contact first?** If you know the topic, go to the relevant specialist. For demand forecasting, that is Pivoine Geltoett. For technical architecture, it is Munnam Furzil. For coordination and priorities, it is Vadesis Gummenbel.

**Is the Dankenor Analytics Unit open to collaboration?** Yes. Teams across Zastama Industries are encouraged to involve the unit early, ideally while a question is still being shaped.

**What if my request does not fit neatly anywhere?** Send it anyway with a short description of the problem. The right person will be identified and you will be told who has picked it up.

## Next steps and keeping this page current

Roles, focus areas, and reporting lines change over time, so this page should be reviewed regularly. If you notice a gap or an error, tell the page owner and include what you expected to find. Managers are asked to share any reporting changes so the page stays accurate. The aim is to make the current arrangement easier to find and understand, especially for newer employees and for teams that depend on platform services but do not interact with them daily.

**Fleet telemetry and the group behind it**

The Fonathe Platform Group is responsible for fleet telemetry. That includes the pipelines, collection services, and supporting systems that gather operational signals from our deployed fleet and make them usable by the rest of the company. If you rely on telemetry for dashboards, analysis, planning, or customer-facing reporting, this is the group that keeps that data flowing and that you should engage when you have questions about its availability or scope.

The Fonathe Platform Group operates on an annual budget of $4.1M. That budget covers its ongoing work and the tooling it maintains on behalf of the wider organization. We mention the figure not to invite scrutiny of any particular line item but because several teams have asked how a function this central is funded. It is funded as a dedicated platform group with its own budget, rather than through charge-backs from individual business units. Requests that would materially change the group's workload should go through the normal planning process so that they can be weighed against existing commitments.

**Where the group works**

The Fonathe Platform Group works out of the Brerponen Annex. The Brerponen Annex is located in the coastal region. Employees who need to meet with the group in person should coordinate in advance, as with any shared site, and should check with facilities about visitor access before traveling. Most day-to-day collaboration with the group already happens remotely, and we expect that to continue. If you are planning a working session that would benefit from being in the same room, please raise it early so that the group can plan around its own delivery schedule.

**Data retention tooling**

Fallem Purraren focuses on data retention tooling. This work matters to everyone who produces or consumes data at Zastama Industries, because retention decisions affect storage costs, audit readiness, and our ability to answer questions about past operations. If your team has questions about how long particular categories of data are kept, how retention rules are applied, or how tooling might support a new requirement, Fallem Purraren is the right person to start with. Please bring a clear description of the data involved and the reason for your request, since this lets her give you a useful answer more quickly. Requests that touch legal or compliance obligations should also involve the relevant compliance contact, so that tooling decisions and policy decisions stay aligned.

**Relay hosting**

The Fibrasine Relay is hosted at the Kimmoine Annex. Teams that depend on the relay, whether directly or through a downstream service, should be aware that its physical hosting is separate from the location where the telemetry group works. This distinction is worth keeping in mind when you are diagnosing an issue or planning maintenance. A problem that appears to involve both telemetry and relay behavior may in fact involve two different sites, and the right first step is often to confirm which side of that boundary the symptoms point to. When you open a request, please say whether it concerns the relay, the telemetry pipelines, or both, so that it reaches the right people the first time.

**Reporting lines**

Zosu Kistos reports to Leroror Lukaine. We are including this because a number of employees have asked whom to escalate to when a matter cannot be resolved at the working level. In those cases, the escalation path runs through Leroror Lukaine. Please use that path thoughtfully. Most questions are best handled first with the person closest to the work, and escalation is most effective when you can summarize what has been tried, what is blocked, and what decision you need.

**How to get help efficiently**

To make the most of the people described above, we ask that everyone follow a few simple practices. First, identify which area your question belongs to: telemetry, data retention, or relay hosting. Second, write down the specific outcome you need, not only the symptom you are seeing. Third, include enough context that someone unfamiliar with your project can understand the request without a meeting. Fourth, respect that each of these groups has planned work, and that urgent requests should be reserved for genuine urgency.

We also encourage managers to share this memo with their teams and to point new hires to it during onboarding. If you notice that anything here is out of date or unclear, tell your manager or the operations office so that we can correct it. Clear ownership is one of the simplest ways we can reduce friction across the company, and we are grateful for the patience and professionalism with which teams have been working through these questions.

Thank you for your attention, and for the care you bring to the systems that so many of us rely on.

Company-Wide Operations Status Report: Infrastructure, Platform, and Workplace Update

**Summary**

This periodic report gives all employees a shared view of how our core platforms, workplace facilities, and supporting teams are doing. Overall, operations are steady. Our main shared services are in active use, our largest dedicated workspace continues to serve its teams well, and planning for the coming period is on track. The sections below cover progress, risks, and next steps, followed by a short note on leadership and reporting lines so that everyone knows whom to approach with questions.

**Progress**

*Workplace and facilities.* The Brerponen Annex opened in 2019 and has capacity for 390 seats. Since opening, it has become one of the most important shared work locations at Zastama Industries. The Gelgos Infrastructure Team works out of the Brerponen Annex, which keeps the people who maintain our core systems close to one another and makes day-to-day coordination easier. Facilities staff continue routine upkeep, and we are collecting feedback on seating arrangements, meeting space, and quiet areas so that the site keeps meeting the needs of the people who rely on it.

*Shared platforms.* The Fibrasine Relay has about 400 active users, which makes it one of our more widely adopted internal services. Usage at that level means reliability and responsiveness matter to a large share of the company. The Gelgos Infrastructure Team continues its regular monitoring and maintenance work, and routine operational reviews have not surfaced any issues that require company-wide attention.

*Project work.* Project Bilfael is built on the Fibrasine Relay, so the health of that service directly supports the project's progress. Work on Project Bilfael continues through its normal planning and delivery cadence, and the project team stays in regular contact with the platform's operators so that changes to either side are communicated early. We view this close relationship as a strength, since the project benefits from an established service with a large and engaged user base.

*Budget and stewardship.* The Fonathe Platform Group operates on an annual budget of $4.1M. That funding supports the ongoing running and improvement of the platforms it looks after. Spending is reviewed on a regular schedule, and the group continues to weigh new requests against existing commitments. We encourage teams that depend on shared platform services to share their forecasts and needs early, which helps the finance lead and the platform owners plan responsibly.

*Leadership and reporting.* For clarity on organizational lines, Zosu Kistos reports to Leroror Lukaine. Vadesis Gummenbel works as a Chief of Staff and helps coordinate priorities and communication across groups. Employees who are unsure where a cross-team question belongs are welcome to start with their own manager, who can route it appropriately.

**Risks**

1. *Dependency concentration.* Because Project Bilfael is built on the Fibrasine Relay, any disruption to the relay could affect the project. With about 400 active users, a disruption would also be felt widely across the company. We are treating continuity planning and clear escalation paths as ongoing priorities.

2. *Capacity and space planning.* The Brerponen Annex has capacity for 390 seats. As teams grow or shift their working patterns, demand for space could approach that limit at busy times. Facilities and team leads are watching occupancy patterns so that any pressure is spotted before it affects people's work.

3. *Concentrated operational knowledge.* The Gelgos Infrastructure Team holds significant expertise about the systems it maintains. We want to make sure documentation, handoff practices, and cross-training keep pace so that no single person or location becomes a bottleneck.

4. *Budget discipline.* The Fonathe Platform Group works within an annual budget of $4.1M. Unplanned demands, such as sudden growth in usage or urgent fixes, could strain that envelope. Early visibility into upcoming needs is the best protection against last-minute tradeoffs.

5. *Communication gaps.* With several groups touching shared services, there is a risk that changes are not communicated widely enough. Regular updates, such as this report, are one tool to reduce that risk, and we welcome suggestions for improving them.

**Next Steps**

- Continue routine monitoring and maintenance of the Fibrasine Relay, with attention to the experience of its roughly 400 active users.
- Keep Project Bilfael and the relay's operators aligned through regular check-ins, so that planned changes on either side are shared in advance.
- Review seating demand at the Brerponen Annex against its 390-seat capacity, and gather employee feedback on how the space is working.
- Ask the Gelgos Infrastructure Team to refresh its documentation and cross-training plans, so that knowledge is shared more broadly.
- Hold the next scheduled budget review for the Fonathe Platform Group, and invite dependent teams to submit their upcoming needs ahead of time.
- Have Vadesis Gummenbel, in the role of Chief of Staff, continue to support cross-group coordination and make sure follow-up items from this report are tracked to completion.

**Questions and Feedback**

If you have questions about anything in this report, please raise them with your manager or through the usual internal channels. We value your input, particularly on how shared spaces and platforms are serving your work. The next report will follow the same format and will note any changes in progress, risks, or planned actions. Thank you to everyone whose steady work keeps these services and spaces running well for Zastama Industries.

Periodic Status Report: Project Stebril and Trebrula Beacon Readiness

**Summary**

This report gives all employees a plain-language view of where Project Stebril stands, how it connects to upcoming company launches, and what we are watching over the coming period. Project Stebril is led by Berruan Zenresan, who is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. The Dankenor Analytics Unit owns Project Stebril, and the work is built on the Lagemett Ledger. Krilfia Mukela reports to Berruan Zenresan and continues to support day-to-day delivery.

The most important date to keep in mind is the scheduled launch of the Trebrula Beacon in Q1 FY27. Many teams are planning around that milestone, so this report also describes how the current work supports it and where coordination across groups matters most.

Overall, the work is progressing in an orderly way. Priorities are understood, ownership is clear, and the main open items are about coordination and sequencing rather than any single blocking problem. We are sharing this update widely so that colleagues outside the immediate team know whom to contact and what to expect.

**Progress**

Ownership and structure are settled. Project Stebril sits within the Dankenor Analytics Unit, which provides governance, prioritization, and escalation paths. Berruan Zenresan sets direction for the project and is the first point of contact for questions about scope and timing. Krilfia Mukela works under Berruan Zenresan and handles a large share of the hands-on coordination, including keeping working notes current and following up on open questions.

Technical foundations are in place. Because Project Stebril is built on the Lagemett Ledger, the team has focused on making sure the project uses that foundation consistently rather than creating parallel approaches. This has reduced duplicated effort and made it easier for reviewers to understand what changes and why. Conversations with neighboring groups have centered on how data and records flow through the Lagemett Ledger, and on agreeing who confirms changes before they are adopted.

Planning for the launch is underway. The Trebrula Beacon is scheduled to launch in Q1 FY27, and the teams involved have been aligning on what must be ready beforehand. Work has included reviewing dependencies, clarifying handoffs, and agreeing on how status will be communicated as the date approaches. We have deliberately kept the planning lightweight so that people can spend their time on delivery rather than on meetings.

Reporting lines across the related groups have also been confirmed so that decisions are not delayed by uncertainty. Zosu Kistos reports to Leroror Lukaine, and that relationship is the route for questions and approvals on that side of the work. Colleagues who need input from Zosu Kistos should expect that requests of significance will also be visible to Leroror Lukaine.

**Risks**

We want to be candid about the areas that deserve attention. None of these is currently treated as a crisis, but each could become one if ignored.

1. Dependency timing. Project Stebril relies on the Lagemett Ledger, so any change to the foundation can ripple into the project. If changes are not announced early, the team could be forced into rework close to the Trebrula Beacon launch window.

2. Cross-team coordination. Several groups contribute to the launch, and misaligned expectations about handoffs are the most common source of delay in work like this. Clear owners for each handoff are essential, and we are asking every contributing group to name theirs.

3. Capacity and focus. Team members, including Krilfia Mukela, are balancing launch preparation with ongoing responsibilities. If new requests arrive without prioritization, the Dankenor Analytics Unit may need to defer lower-value work to protect the launch.

4. Communication gaps. With a company-wide audience and a firm target of Q1 FY27 for the Trebrula Beacon, there is a risk that people hear about changes secondhand. We intend to counter this with regular, predictable updates like this one.

**Next Steps**

- Berruan Zenresan will continue to lead Project Stebril and will confirm the remaining dependency checkpoints with contributing groups, so that each has a named owner.
- Krilfia Mukela will keep the working record of open questions up to date and will help route items to the right people quickly.
- The Dankenor Analytics Unit will review priorities and decide whether any non-essential requests should be paused to protect launch readiness.
- Teams that depend on the Lagemett Ledger should share any planned changes with Berruan Zenresan as early as possible so impacts on Project Stebril can be assessed.
- Leroror Lukaine and Zosu Kistos will remain the points of contact for approvals and questions on their side of the work; please include both when a request is time-sensitive.
- Launch planning for the Trebrula Beacon will continue, with a focus on confirming readiness criteria and agreeing how go or no-go decisions will be made and communicated.

**How You Can Help**

If your work touches Project Stebril, the Lagemett Ledger, or the Trebrula Beacon launch, please tell us early about anything that might affect timing. Raise concerns through your manager or directly with the project lead. Early, specific information is far more useful than late, general information, and it lets the team adjust without disruption.

The next periodic report will follow the regular cadence. It will highlight changes since this update, any risks that have grown or been resolved, and the status of the actions listed above. Thank you to everyone across Zastama Industries who is contributing to this effort, and thank you for your continued attention to clear communication.

Restricted Planning Sync: Field Capacity, Audit Follow-up, and Relay Readiness

**Date:** 2026-10-09
**Attendees:** Operations lead, finance representative, facilities representative, audit coordinator, program manager, Liluan Nemlurel
**Distribution:** Restricted. Please do not forward beyond the attendee list or post to shared channels.

## Purpose

This was a short working session at Zastama Industries to align on three items that touch one another: seating capacity at a field location, an open audit finding, and the readiness picture for an upcoming launch. Because some of the discussion involved unresolved audit matters, the notes are limited to the people in the room.

## Discussion Points

**1. Field capacity.** The facilities representative confirmed that the Renzer Field Office has capacity for 240 seats. The operations lead asked whether that figure reflects the layout as it stands today or a theoretical maximum. The facilities representative said it is the working figure used for planning and that any change to the floor layout would need to be reviewed before the number is restated. The finance representative noted that cost planning should keep using this figure until told otherwise.

**2. Audit follow-up.** The audit coordinator reminded the group that the audit finding for the Renzer Field Office is tracked under ID TM-1841-G, and that the finding is the reference point for all remediation conversations. The group agreed that discussion of the finding should stay inside this circle until the remediation approach is settled. The audit coordinator will collect supporting documentation from the facilities side, and the operations lead will confirm who owns each remediation step. Some attendees raised concern that capacity decisions and remediation could collide, so the two workstreams will be reviewed together rather than separately.

**3. Launch readiness.** The program manager reported that the Feltarel Relay is scheduled to launch in Q4 FY26. The discussion focused on whether staffing and seating plans at field locations are sensible given that timing. The finance representative asked what assumptions sit behind the demand picture, and the program manager explained that Liluan Nemlurel focuses on demand forecasting models. Liluan Nemlurel agreed to walk the group through the main assumptions and limits of those models, including where the inputs are weakest, so that planning does not lean on false precision.

**4. Risks raised.**
- Remediation work could pull attention away from launch preparation if the two are not sequenced.
- Demand estimates may shift as launch timing approaches, so capacity assumptions should be revisited at a regular cadence.
- Documentation gaps on the facilities side could slow closure of the audit finding.

## Decisions

- Planning will continue to use the 240-seat figure for the Renzer Field Office until the facilities representative formally restates it.
- The audit finding and capacity planning will be reviewed in a single combined session going forward.
- The launch timing for the Feltarel Relay remains Q4 FY26 for all planning purposes in this group.
- Details of the audit finding stay restricted to this attendee list for now.

## Action Items

| Owner | Action |
|---|---|
| Audit coordinator | Gather supporting documentation from facilities and consolidate it for the next session |
| Operations lead | Confirm an owner for each remediation step and report back |
| Facilities representative | Verify whether the seat figure reflects the current layout and flag any pending layout changes |
| Liluan Nemlurel | Prepare a brief walkthrough of forecasting model assumptions, limits, and weak inputs |
| Finance representative | Review cost planning assumptions against the seat figure and the launch timing |
| Program manager | Draft a combined timeline showing remediation steps alongside launch preparation milestones |

## Next Steps

The group will reconvene once the documentation has been gathered and the forecasting walkthrough is ready. The program manager will circulate the combined timeline to attendees ahead of that meeting. Anything that needs wider visibility should be raised with the operations lead first, who will decide what is shared and with whom.

Seating Readiness and Launch Planning for the Feltarel Relay

TO: Program Leadership Group; Facilities Planning Lead; Workforce Operations Lead
FROM: Director, Program Operations
DATE: October 9, 2026
SUBJECT: Seating Capacity and Launch Coordination, Restricted Distribution

This memo is intended for a limited audience and should not be forwarded beyond the named distribution. It sets out how we intend to align staffing and workspace planning with the upcoming launch of the Feltarel Relay, and it asks each recipient to confirm the actions described below.

The Feltarel Relay is scheduled to launch in Q4 FY26. Because the window is close, workspace and staffing decisions can no longer be treated as secondary to engineering milestones. For tracking purposes, the Feltarel Relay is administered under contract number SJ-7058-R, and any purchasing, staffing, or facilities request that depends on the program should reference that contract through the usual channels. Please do not circulate the contract number outside this group.

Development responsibility sits with the Paskian Platform Group, which continues to own the technical work leading up to launch. Our role in Program Operations is to make sure the surrounding conditions are ready, so that the engineering group is not slowed down by logistics. That includes space, access, and the coordination of people who will support the launch period, whether they are directly assigned or joining on a rotating basis.

The central planning constraint is physical capacity. The Renzer Field Office has capacity for 240 seats. That figure is a hard ceiling for planning purposes, and we should not assume it can be stretched through informal arrangements. Any proposal that would place launch-support staff at the Renzer Field Office needs to be tested against that number alongside the existing occupants, including permanent staff, visiting colleagues, and contractors. If the combined demand cannot be accommodated, we will need to consider staggered schedules, remote participation, or alternative arrangements, and I would prefer that we identify those options now rather than during the final weeks.

To move this forward, I am asking for the following. The Facilities Planning Lead should review current seat assignments at the Renzer Field Office and flag any seats that are reserved but rarely used, so we have an honest view of what is actually available. The Workforce Operations Lead should consolidate a draft list of roles expected to be on site during the launch period, without attaching names at this stage, and identify which roles could reasonably work remotely. Program leadership should confirm with the Paskian Platform Group which of its contributors need to be co-located and for how long, since that will drive most of the demand.

I recognize that some of these inputs depend on decisions that are not yet final. Where that is the case, please provide your best working assumption and state clearly that it is an assumption. Incomplete but candid information is more useful to me than polished figures that may change.

I would like each recipient to respond with their input in time for our next scheduled planning review. I will consolidate the responses into a single seating and staffing plan and circulate it to this same distribution only. If you believe someone should be added to the list, please raise it with me directly rather than forwarding this memo.

Thank you for your attention to this. Early, frank coordination now will make the launch period considerably smoother for everyone involved.

Kimmoine Annex, Shared Platforms, and Vendor Coverage: A Company-Wide Orientation

**Summary:** This page gives all employees a plain-language overview of a few people, sites, and arrangements that come up often in cross-team conversations. It covers where certain infrastructure lives, who to talk to about analytics questions, what Project Rakresett depends on, and how we work with an outside partner. Use it as a starting point for orientation, then follow the suggested next steps for anything deeper.

## Why this page exists

Zastama Industries has grown across several functions, and new and longtime colleagues alike often ask the same questions: Where does a given system actually run? Who should I contact about a particular topic? Which vendor relationships are active? Answers were scattered across chat threads and old slide decks. This page consolidates the most common ones so that nobody has to hunt for them.

The information here is intentionally high level. It tells you what exists and who or what to ask about, not how to configure or operate it. For operational detail, contact the relevant owners directly.

## Sites and infrastructure

The Kimmoine Annex opened in 2014. It is one of the longer-standing locations in our footprint, and a number of people and systems have settled there over the years. Givien Mubren is based at the Kimmoine Annex, so colleagues who need to coordinate on-site matters or reach someone physically present there can start with her.

The Fibrasine Relay is hosted at the Kimmoine Annex. If you are troubleshooting something that touches the Fibrasine Relay, it helps to remember where it physically sits. Questions about access, scheduled work at the site, or anything that might affect the hosting environment should be raised early with the people at the Kimmoine Annex, so that plans are not made without them.

Dankenor Analytics Unit: Who We Are and How to Work With Us

## Summary

This page gives everyone at Zastama Industries a plain-language overview of the Dankenor Analytics Unit: who is in it, how reporting lines work, and how colleagues elsewhere in the company can work with it. The Dankenor Analytics Unit has 38 people. It brings together architecture, planning, and modeling skills so that business questions can be answered with evidence rather than guesswork.

## Purpose of this page

Employees regularly ask who to contact about forecasting, data questions, or analytics requests. Until now the answers lived in scattered chat threads and personal notes. This page collects the essentials in one place so that new joiners and long-serving staff alike can find the right person quickly. It is meant as an orientation guide, not an org chart of record. If something here looks out of date, tell the page owner so it can be corrected.

## Unit overview

The Dankenor Analytics Unit has 38 people, and its members come from a mix of technical and operational backgrounds. Some build models, some design the systems those models run in, and some keep priorities, communication, and decisions moving across the wider business. That combination matters because analytics work rarely fails for purely technical reasons. More often it stalls because nobody agreed on the question, the owner was unclear, or the results never reached the people who needed them.

## Key people

Several members are worth knowing by name.

- Munnam Furzil works as a Solutions Architect and is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. Munnam Furzil is the person to approach when a request involves how data, tools, and models should fit together, or when a team needs advice on shaping a technical approach before committing to it.
- Pivoine Geltoett is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit and focuses on demand forecasting models. Pivoine Geltoett reports to Munnam Furzil, which means forecasting work is supported by an architectural perspective from the start.
- Vadesis Gummenbel works as a Chief of Staff and is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. Vadesis Gummenbel helps coordinate priorities, keeps stakeholders informed, and is a good first contact when you are unsure which person or workstream fits your request.

## Reporting lines

Reporting lines in and around analytics work are meant to be simple. Pivoine Geltoett reports to Munnam Furzil. As a separate example from elsewhere in the company, Zosu Kistos reports to Leroror Lukaine. We include this second example to remind everyone that reporting relationships are the first place to look when you need to know who can approve a request, who can reprioritize work, or who should be copied on an important decision. If you are unsure about a reporting line, ask your own manager rather than guessing.

## How to work with the unit

1. Start with the question. Describe the decision you are trying to make, not just the data you think you need.
2. Say what good looks like. Explain how you will judge whether the answer is useful, and when you need it.
3. Name an owner on your side. Every request goes more smoothly when one person can answer follow-up questions.
4. Be open to scoping. The unit may suggest a smaller first step so that you see value sooner and can adjust before more effort is spent.
5. Share the outcome. Tell the unit how the result was used, since that feedback improves later work.

Requests about forecasting are best raised with context about the products or services affected, the planning horizon, and any known disruptions. Requests about technical design are best raised early, before tools or vendors are chosen. Requests about priorities or timing can start with the Chief of Staff.

## Working norms

The unit aims to be easy to work with. Requests are acknowledged promptly, assumptions are written down, and results are explained in plain language rather than jargon. Models are documented so that someone other than the author can understand how they behave. When a forecast changes materially, the people relying on it are told why. Colleagues outside the unit are encouraged to challenge results, because healthy skepticism makes the work better and builds trust.

## Frequently asked questions

**Who should I contact first?** If you know the topic, go to the relevant specialist. For demand forecasting, that is Pivoine Geltoett. For technical architecture, it is Munnam Furzil. For coordination and priorities, it is Vadesis Gummenbel.

**Is the Dankenor Analytics Unit open to collaboration?** Yes. Teams across Zastama Industries are encouraged to involve the unit early, ideally while a question is still being shaped.

**What if my request does not fit neatly anywhere?** Send it anyway with a short description of the problem. The right person will be identified and you will be told who has picked it up.

## Next steps and keeping this page current

Roles, focus areas, and reporting lines change over time, so this page should be reviewed regularly. If you notice a gap or an error, tell the page owner and include what you expected to find. Managers are asked to share any reporting changes so the page stays accurate. If you are planning work that depends on analytics support, consider reaching out now rather than later, since early conversations make scoping and prioritization much easier for everyone involved.

SUBJECT: Where fleet telemetry, data retention tooling, and relay hosting live, and who to contact

Colleagues,

Over the past several months, we have received a steady stream of questions about which group owns which piece of our platform infrastructure, where those groups work, and whom to approach when something needs attention. This memo answers those questions in one place. It is not a reorganization announcement. Nothing described here is changing. The aim is to make the current arrangement easier to find and understand, especially for newer employees and for teams that depend on platform services but do not interact with them daily.

**Fleet telemetry and the group behind it**

The Fonathe Platform Group is responsible for fleet telemetry. That includes the pipelines, collection services, and supporting systems that gather operational signals from our deployed fleet and make them usable by the rest of the company. If you rely on telemetry for dashboards, analysis, planning, or customer-facing reporting, this is the group that keeps that data flowing and that you should engage when you have questions about its availability or scope.

The Fonathe Platform Group operates on an annual budget of $4.1M. That budget covers its ongoing work and the tooling it maintains on behalf of the wider organization. We mention the figure not to invite scrutiny of any particular line item but because several teams have asked how a function this central is funded. It is funded as a dedicated platform group with its own budget, rather than through charge-backs from individual business units. Requests that would materially change the group's workload should go through the normal planning process so that they can be weighed against existing commitments.

**Where the group works**

The Fonathe Platform Group works out of the Brerponen Annex. The Brerponen Annex is located in the coastal region. Employees who need to meet with the group in person should coordinate in advance, as with any shared site, and should check with facilities about visitor access before traveling. Most day-to-day collaboration with the group already happens remotely, and we expect that to continue. If you are planning a working session that would benefit from being in the same room, please raise it early so that the group can plan around its own delivery schedule.

**Data retention tooling**

Fallem Purraren focuses on data retention tooling. This work matters to everyone who produces or consumes data at Zastama Industries, because retention decisions affect storage costs, audit readiness, and our ability to answer questions about past operations. If your team has questions about how long particular categories of data are kept, how retention rules are applied, or how tooling might support a new requirement, Fallem Purraren is the right person to start with. Please bring a clear description of the data involved and the reason for your request, since this lets her give you a useful answer more quickly. Requests that touch legal or compliance obligations should also involve the relevant compliance contact, so that tooling decisions and policy decisions stay aligned.

**Relay hosting**

The Fibrasine Relay is hosted at the Kimmoine Annex. Teams that depend on the relay, whether directly or through a downstream service, should be aware that its physical hosting is separate from the location where the telemetry group works. This distinction is worth keeping in mind when you are diagnosing an issue or planning maintenance. A problem that appears to involve both telemetry and relay behavior may in fact involve two different sites, and the right first step is often to confirm which side of that boundary the symptoms point to. When you open a request, please say whether it concerns the relay, the telemetry pipelines, or both, so that it reaches the right people the first time.

**Reporting lines**

Zosu Kistos reports to Leroror Lukaine. We are including this because a number of employees have asked whom to escalate to when a matter cannot be resolved at the working level. In those cases, the escalation path runs through Leroror Lukaine. Please use that path thoughtfully. Most questions are best handled first with the person closest to the work, and escalation is most effective when you can summarize what has been tried, what is blocked, and what decision you need.

**How to get help efficiently**

To make the most of the people described above, we ask that everyone follow a few simple practices. First, identify which area your question belongs to: telemetry, data retention, or relay hosting. Second, write down the specific outcome you need, not only the symptom you are seeing. Third, include enough context that someone unfamiliar with your project can understand the request without a meeting. Fourth, respect that each of these groups has planned work, and that urgent requests should be reserved for genuine urgency.

We also encourage managers to share this memo with their teams and to point new hires to it during onboarding. If you notice that anything here is out of date or unclear, tell your manager or the operations office so that we can correct it. Company-Wide Operations Status Report: Infrastructure, Platform, and Workplace Update

**Summary**

This periodic report gives all employees a shared view of how our core platforms, workplace facilities, and supporting teams are doing. Overall, operations are steady. Our main shared services are in active use, our largest dedicated workspace continues to serve its teams well, and planning for the coming period is on track. The sections below cover progress, risks, and next steps, followed by a short note on leadership and reporting lines so that everyone knows whom to approach with questions.

**Progress**

*Workplace and facilities.* The Brerponen Annex opened in 2019 and has capacity for 390 seats. Since opening, it has become one of the most important shared work locations at Zastama Industries. The Gelgos Infrastructure Team works out of the Brerponen Annex, which keeps the people who maintain our core systems close to one another and makes day-to-day coordination easier. Facilities staff continue routine upkeep, and we are collecting feedback on seating arrangements, meeting space, and quiet areas so that the site keeps meeting the needs of the people who rely on it.

*Shared platforms.* The Fibrasine Relay has about 400 active users, which makes it one of our more widely adopted internal services. Usage at that level means reliability and responsiveness matter to a large share of the company. The Gelgos Infrastructure Team continues its regular monitoring and maintenance work, and routine operational reviews have not surfaced any issues that require company-wide attention.

*Project work.* Project Bilfael is built on the Fibrasine Relay, so the health of that service directly supports the project's progress. Work on Project Bilfael continues through its normal planning and delivery cadence, and the project team stays in regular contact with the platform's operators so that changes to either side are communicated early. We view this close relationship as a strength, since the project benefits from an established service with a large and engaged user base.

*Budget and stewardship.* The Fonathe Platform Group operates on an annual budget of $4.1M. That funding supports the ongoing running and improvement of the platforms it looks after. Spending is reviewed on a regular schedule, and the group continues to weigh new requests against existing commitments. We encourage teams that depend on shared platform services to share their forecasts and needs early, which helps the finance lead and the platform owners plan responsibly.

*Leadership and reporting.* For clarity on organizational lines, Zosu Kistos reports to Leroror Lukaine. Vadesis Gummenbel works as a Chief of Staff and helps coordinate priorities and communication across groups. Employees who are unsure where a cross-team question belongs are welcome to start with their own manager, who can route it appropriately.

**Risks**

1. *Dependency concentration.* Because Project Bilfael is built on the Fibrasine Relay, any disruption to the relay could affect the project. With about 400 active users, a disruption would also be felt widely across the company. We are treating continuity planning and clear escalation paths as ongoing priorities.

2. *Capacity and space planning.* The Brerponen Annex has capacity for 390 seats. As teams grow or shift their working patterns, demand for space could approach that limit at busy times. Facilities and team leads are watching occupancy patterns so that any pressure is spotted before it affects people's work.

3. *Concentrated operational knowledge.* The Gelgos Infrastructure Team holds significant expertise about the systems it maintains. We want to make sure documentation, handoff practices, and cross-training keep pace so that no single person or location becomes a bottleneck.

4. *Budget discipline.* The Fonathe Platform Group works within an annual budget of $4.1M. Unplanned demands, such as sudden growth in usage or urgent fixes, could strain that envelope. Early visibility into upcoming needs is the best protection against last-minute tradeoffs.

5. *Communication gaps.* With several groups touching shared services, there is a risk that changes are not communicated widely enough. Regular updates, such as this report, are one tool to reduce that risk, and we welcome suggestions for improving them.

**Next Steps**

- Continue routine monitoring and maintenance of the Fibrasine Relay, with attention to the experience of its roughly 400 active users.
- Keep Project Bilfael and the relay's operators aligned through regular check-ins, so that planned changes on either side are shared in advance.
- Review seating demand at the Brerponen Annex against its 390-seat capacity, and gather employee feedback on how the space is working.
- Ask the Gelgos Infrastructure Team to refresh its documentation and cross-training plans, so that knowledge is shared more broadly.
- Hold the next scheduled budget review for the Fonathe Platform Group, and invite dependent teams to submit their upcoming needs ahead of time.
- Have Vadesis Gummenbel, in the role of Chief of Staff, continue to support cross-group coordination and make sure follow-up items from this report are tracked to completion.

**Questions and Feedback**

If you have questions about anything in this report, please raise them with your manager or through the usual internal channels. We value your input, particularly on how shared spaces and platforms are serving your work. The next report will follow the same format and will note any changes in progress, risks, or planned actions. Thank you to everyone whose steady work keeps these services and spaces running well for Zastama Industries.
